groups.title: Serverless Functions Concepts
groups.question: Your static site needs a contact form and a weather widget that uses a paid API key. Explain how serverless functions handle this and what to watch out for.

followUps.Serverless execution model and cold star: What is a cold start and why does it happen?
followUps.HTTP request and response structure in s: What does a serverless handler receive and return?
followUps.Environment variables and secrets manage: Why must the API key live in the function and not the frontend?

evidence.text: Serverless functions run in short-lived containers started on demand.
They keep no state between requests, so data must live in a database or other service.
The first request to an idle function waits for it to start, which adds latency.

notEnough: Only saying serverless means no servers.

evidence.text: The handler receives the request with its headers, query parameters and body.
It returns a status code, headers and a body.
It works like a normal HTTP request and response.

notEnough: Only saying it is a function.

evidence.text: Anything in client code is visible to users.
Functions read secrets from environment variables set in the hosting dashboard.
The key is used only on the server, so it never reaches the browser.

notEnough: Only saying to keep keys secret.

groups.title: Error Handling and Rate Limits
groups.question: Your serverless function calls an external API that sometimes returns 429, and the browser blocks calls to your function from another domain. Explain how you would handle both.

followUps.Rate limiting strategies and handling 42: What does a 429 mean and how should your code respond?
followUps.CORS configuration for serverless functi: What must the function return for a cross-origin browser request?

evidence.text: 429 means you have sent too many requests in a time window.
Retry after waiting, with longer waits each time.
Queuing or caching requests avoids hitting the limit in the first place.
The response needs an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header for the allowed site.
The function must also answer preflight OPTIONS requests.
Only trusted origins should be allowed.

groups.title: Calling External APIs Securely
groups.question: Your site's contact form and search use third-party APIs with secret keys, and you have no backend server. Explain how you would call these APIs safely.

followUps.Proxying third-party API calls through s: How does a serverless proxy keep an API key off the client?
followUps.Form submission handling without a backe: How would you handle a contact form without your own server?

evidence.text: The client calls your function instead of the third-party API.
The function adds the secret key from its environment and forwards the request.
The function can also validate input and limit what clients may request.

notEnough: Only saying you use a proxy.

evidence.text: The form posts to a serverless function or a platform form service.
The function validates the input and rejects bad submissions.
It then sends an email or stores the message through an external service.

notEnough: Only saying you use Netlify Forms.

groups.title: Next.js API Routes and Edge Functions
groups.question: You are adding API endpoints to a Next.js site and want to redirect users by country before pages load. Explain route handlers and edge functions.

followUps.Next.js Route Handlers as serverless API: How do you create an API endpoint in the Next.js App Router?
followUps.Edge Functions for low-latency personali: What are edge functions good for and what limits do they have?

evidence.text: A route file under the app directory exports functions named after HTTP methods.
On Vercel these become serverless functions.
They can use the same code and environment as the rest of the app.

notEnough: Only saying you add an api folder.

evidence.text: Edge functions run on servers close to the user.
They suit quick tasks like redirects, A/B tests and auth checks.
They run in a lighter runtime that lacks some Node.js APIs.

notEnough: Only saying edge functions are fast.
